title: Systematic Review of Machine Learning Approaches in Personal Financial Management Systems
authors: D'Souza, S.; Narasimha Murthy, S.; Bademavidi, V. V.
tldr: A systematic literature review (2018-2024) of machine learning approaches used in personal financial management systems, covering 45 papers across clustering, classification, regression, and deep learning methods.
problem_and_motivation: Personal financial management systems (PFMS) are essential for improving financial well-being, but there is no consolidated understanding of which ML approaches are most effective across different PFMS tasks (budgeting, forecasting, fraud detection, etc.). The rapid growth of ML in finance has led to fragmented research.
approach: Conducted a systematic literature review following PRISMA guidelines on papers from 2018-2024.
Searched Scopus, Web of Science, and IEEE Xplore databases with keywords related to personal finance and machine learning.
Screened 15,176 initial records to 45 eligible papers through title, abstract, and full-text screening.
Extracted data on ML approaches, financial tasks, performance metrics, and datasets.
Categorized financial tasks into six groups: financial literacy, personal budgeting, spending prediction, investment, personal loans, and savings.
Synthesized findings by ML technique families: clustering, ensemble methods, neural networks, and reinforcement learning.
Identified research gaps and proposed directions for future work.
findings: Clustering (especially K-Means) and ensemble methods (Random Forest, XGBoost) are most widely used for personal budgeting and spending prediction.
Deep learning (LSTM, GRU, CNNs) dominates forecasting tasks including stock price prediction and portfolio optimization.
num: The majority of papers (25%) address spending prediction, followed by investment (24%) and personal budgeting (14%).
Neural networks achieve highest accuracy for complex forecasting but require large, high-quality datasets.
Random Forest achieves best overall accuracy for classification tasks and handles high-dimensional financial data well.
Key gaps include limited focus on financial literacy improvement and savings management in PFMS research.
Privacy-preserving ML and explainable AI are emerging but underexplored in PFMS contexts.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This SLR provides a comprehensive mapping of ML approaches to PFMS tasks, identifying that clustering and ensemble methods dominate personal budgeting, while deep learning dominates forecasting. It highlights the underrepresentation of financial literacy and savings-focused research, and identifies privacy-preserving ML and explainable AI as critical gaps. The paper offers a structured reference for PFMS researchers to select appropriate ML techniques for their target tasks.
directly_justifies: Random Forest achieves best overall accuracy for classification tasks in PFMS.
LSTM and GRU perform best for sequential forecasting tasks like spending prediction.
Spending prediction is the most researched PFMS task in the ML literature.
limits: Limited to papers from 2018-2024; earlier foundation work not covered. [acknowledged]
Only three databases were searched; grey literature excluded. [acknowledged]
SLR does not include empirical comparison or meta-analysis across papers. [unacknowledged]
topic_relevance.topic_mapping_rationale: Systematic scan across all 14 topic domains was performed. Domains 4.A (landscape), 6.A (spending prediction), and 14.A (ML approaches) were flagged as highly relevant because the SLR directly maps ML techniques to PFMS tasks. Domain 5.A was flagged as medium relevance because clustering for user profiling is covered but not as a primary focus. Domain 8.A was flagged as medium relevance because fraud detection appears as a covered task. Domains 1-3 (Filipino context, cultural practices) were rejected as the review is international in scope with no Philippines-specific analysis. Domain 7 (budgeting), 9 (income), 10 (privacy), and 13 (savings/debt) were covered at a high level as PFMS tasks but without depth sufficient for inclusion. Domain 11-12 (engagement, evaluation) were rejected because system evaluation and user engagement are not the focus of the SLR.

limitations: Limited to 3 databases and publications from 2018-2024 only. [acknowledged]
No empirical comparison or meta-analysis of performance across studies. [unacknowledged]
Does not cover PFMS implementation details or user experience aspects. [unacknowledged]
remember_this: Clustering + ensemble methods dominate budgeting tasks; deep learning dominates forecasting.
Spending prediction is the most common PFMS task studied with ML (25%).
Random Forest performs best overall for classification in PFMS.
Financial literacy improvement and savings management are underexplored in ML-PFMS research.
